newsitem.title: FRANCE: France to ask EU to join Zaire aid airlift.
newsitem.headline: France to ask EU to join Zaire aid airlift.

text.p: France said on Wednesday it would ask its European Union partners to help it to organise an airlift of humanitarian aid supplies to the northeast Zaire city of Kisangani, the target of a rebel offensive.
Foreign Ministy spokesman Yves Doutriaux also said the possibility of sending a military force to the area would have to be again considered if there was no ceasefire soon.

"We are going to propose today and tomorrow to our European partners at meetings in Brussels on Africa that the European Union get involved in creating a sort of airlift to Kisangani and eastern Zaire," Doutriaux told a news briefing.
A French cargo aircraft was already on its way to Zaire with supplies following another plane which flew there earlier this week, he said.
"If a ceasefire does not take hold soon, then we will again have to consider sending a (military) force," he added.

Doutriaux declined comment on a French newspaper report that Paris was considering a joint force with Belgian, Dutch and Egyptian troops to provide protection for relief organisations seeking to aid Rwandan Hutu refugees in the war zone.

France, which long sought to involve the United States and its unmatched heavy airlift capacity, apparently gave up after talks with U.S. Assistant Secretary of State for African development George Moose which Doutriaux said took place in Brussels on Tuesday.

Rebel leader Laurent Kabila, whose forces are advancing on Kisangani with the aim of toppling Zairean President Mobutu Sese Seko, has accepted a U.N. peace plan as a basis for talks but rejected its call for a ceasefire.
French President Jacques Chirac on Tuesday denounced a "conspiracy of silence" on Zaire and appealed to the international community to force a ceasefire and take emergency humanitarian action.

Government spokesman Alain Lamassoure said Chirac told a cabinet meeting: "The humanitarian situation in Zaire is tragic. No one can ignore it any longer. No one can remain indifferent. We have to ask if there is not a sort of conspiracy of silence."
But critics say France's other motive is to block the rebel advance and save Mobutu, long allied to Paris.
Mobutu's son, Mobutu Nzanga, told Reuters in Paris the Tutsi forces would face their first real battle with the Zairean army if they tried to seize Kisangani, formerly Stanleyville.

Zaire's poorly-equipped, mercenary-backed army has so far put up only token resistance against the five-month rebel advance from Zaire's eastern borders and some analysts doubt if it has the morale to rally to defend Kisangani.
Mobutu, convalescing in his French Riviera mansion after prostate cancer surgery in Switzerland last year, is due to return to Zaire late this week, his son said.
His son also renewed charges that Uganda, Burundi and Rwanda were directing the uprising, a charge they deny.
